newsitem.title: GREECE: EU SOCIALISTS WANT BETTER COORDINATION OF ECON POLICY.
newsitem.headline: EU SOCIALISTS WANT BETTER COORDINATION OF ECON POLICY.

text.p: European Union Socialist officials said on Sunday that a special mechanism should be created to better coordinate EU economic policies and ensure consistency between monetary and other economic policy targets.

"There is a vacuum in the planning of the economic policy within the EU. The EU central bank, the independece of which is guaranteed, is not operating within a consistent framework of economic policy goals as it happens in member states," a joint declaration after a weekend meeting in Athens said.

The meeting was hosted by Greek National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou and participants included former EU Commission Pressident Jacques Delors, the finance ministers of Italy, Finland and Portugal and officials from Austria, Germany, Ireland, and Luxembourg.

Papandoniou said the participants agreed to propose the creation of an "Economic Coordination Pact" which will be equal to the Stability Pact and determine the role of EU governments in the decision making concerning economic policy targets.
"Our target is that in the Luxembourg summit in December we will have a text which will determine the role of the governments in the planning of EU economic policy," he told a news conference.

Political influence over monetary policy matters has been a thorny issue within the EU, with some officials advocating that the opinion of governments must also be taken into account when it comes to important monetary policy decisions.

Finance deputy minister Nikos Christodoulakis told Reuters that this would not affect the independence of the central bank but will "hold it politically accountable" for the effect of monetary policy decisions on the economies of member states.
Papandoniou suggested that EU governments could take decisions allowing the violation of certain monetary targets under special circumstances such as a recession.
Papandoniou appeared confident that the proposal for the formation of the "Economic Cooperation Pact" would be backed by his French and British counterparts and could even be endorsed by Germany.
"These things take time. The Athens meeting was the first step but we have a long road ahead of us," he said.
